title: The Willow Creek Signal Flags
markdown:
In Willow Creek, cozy as a squirrel’s nest, messages that used to arrive like morning dew had gone as scattered as dandelion seed. The Berry Festival was almost a secret to some cottages and a rumour to others. Farmer Giles, bless his forgetful heart, had promised his plumpest pumpkin to two families and then wondered why both arrived with baskets. The village felt like a jumbled ball of yarn.

Tara, whose mind sparked with numbers and riddles, wore her favourite tweed even on warm days, in case the pockets held a clue. Sprig, a frog emerald as new leaves, felt the tangle too. “Ribbit. Beatrice the badger expects a song-sharing party and thinks no one is coming. She’ll be as sad as a rainy Tuesday.”

Tara tapped her chin; snail-shell lines appeared. “We must find why. Faster, perhaps?” Spectacles set. They tried. Her legs blurred, pigtails like brown flags. Sprig’s hops were grand. Notes reached Mr. Fitzwilliam the baker, whose shop always smelled of cinnamon, and Mrs. Higgins the weaver, whose threads shimmered like a rainbow. Confusion stayed. Old Mrs. Gable’s knitting needles went to young Timmy instead of his grandmother. Honey nearly ran out because a message arrived after the pot was already scraped. Speed was not the leak. The system itself was slow: one runner, one hop, one tired pair of legs at a time. A note could be perfect and still arrive after the party had gone home.

One sunny afternoon in Dr. Kellan’s garden, Tara watched a climbing vine. It did not only go straight up. Tendrils, delicate and sticky, reached for the trellis, wrapped, connected, strengthened the climb like tiny helpful hands. She sketched the joins before she spoke. “Sprig. It isn’t one long stem. It’s sharing progress with itself. Connected.”

Dr. Kellan ambled by, beard like ancient trees, pockets rustling facts, spectacles on the end of his nose. “Observing. A vine holds a lesson if you let it.”

Tara showed her notebook. The vine on the page looked like a map more than a plant. “It finds its way, and each part helps the others. A path that talks to itself. Could village messages work like that?”

He chuckled, dry leaves on a path. “A network. Whisper down a line and each person is a node, passing along. Your village can do that with something that does not get tired of running. Something visible.”

He led them to a hill overlooking the creek. From above, the roofs looked a little disorganized, as if the lanes had been arguing. “A bright flag here. Another on Mrs. Higgins’s cottage. Another at the baker’s. Each flag able to see the next.”

Tara’s thoughts linked like quick bright joins. “A message to the far side: raise a flag on the hill; the baker’s roof answers in another colour; it passes on. A relay. No one has to run the whole way.”

They sat in the grass and designed colours and shapes for distance. Crimson for urgent. Sky-blue for meadow gathering. Yellow for celebration. Green for ordinary errands. Sprig tested a scrap of yellow against the oak leaves and said it still shouted. They placed the flags on rooftops, poles, oak branches, a chain of sight-lines. A sender raised the first. That flag only needed to know the next, not the whole story. Position and colour did the rest. Tara numbered the stations in her notebook so no one would invent a shortcut that skipped the baker and left the square in the dark.

The next morning Farmer Giles announced a surprise double-pumpkin sale. Three crimson flags in sequence: hill, baker, square. People arrived in time for the second prize pumpkin, baskets already open. Beatrice’s party travelled as a cascade of yellow from tree to tree; voices arrived on the hour, a cricket choir, and Beatrice stopped looking at the empty chairs. Mrs. Gable’s needles reached the right grandmother on a run of gentle green. Timmy, who had been practising with the wrong pair, looked almost disappointed.

“Fast again,” Sprig hopped, nearly a daisy. “Faster than a dragonfly.”

Tara watched the silent colourful conversation. A crimson came down. A green went up two roofs later. “Each flag is a part. They hold to the next, like a chain.” She did not compare the stars or the roots of all things. She sketched the sight-lines again, neater, so the next festival would not depend on Giles’s memory.

Kellan’s smile was spring sun. He left the oaks to their own weather. Tara and Sprig sat on the hill until the last yellow came down, then folded one spare flag for Beatrice, in case a song needed a second verse. The yarn of the village, for the moment, had an order you could see from the ridge.
